what: A distributed lock lets many servers agree that only one of them does a job at a time. It is usually a lease: a lock that expires on its own after a TTL.
like: Like a meeting room booking that expires: you hold the room for 30 minutes, and if you vanish, the booking ends so others can use it.
why: Stops two servers doing the same job twice, like sending today's emails
Protects a shared resource that cannot handle two writers at once
Leases free the lock on their own if the holder crashes

steps.d: Scheduler A asks the lock service for a named lock, such as jobs:2026-10-28. In Redis this is SET key random-value NX PX 30000 - set only if absent, expire in 30 s.
The lock lives only for its TTL. The holder renews it (keep-alive) while working. If it crashes, the lease runs out and the lock frees itself.
Each grant comes with a number that only goes up, like 33 then 34. In etcd or ZooKeeper the key's revision or zxid can play this part.
The holder sends its token with every write. The store remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects anything older.
Scheduler B tries, sees the lock is taken and either waits with a random delay or skips this run, because A already has it covered.
A deletes the key only if it still holds its own random value, so it never removes a lock that someone else now owns.

choices.d: If a double run only wastes work, one Redis key is enough. If a double run corrupts data, use a consensus store plus fencing tokens.
Long enough for the job plus renewals, short enough that a crash does not block others for long. Renew well before expiry.
Redis for speed, etcd or ZooKeeper for consensus-backed safety, Postgres advisory locks when the work is already in that database.
Try-lock and skip suits schedulers. Blocking waits suit short critical sections. Retry with random jitter so contenders do not collide again.
Often better: make the work safe to repeat with a unique key or upsert, so a double run does no harm and no lock is needed.

instead.why: Advisory locks or a unique constraint in the database you already run
A queue hands each job to one consumer, so no lock needed
SET NX PX for cheap, best-effort efficiency locks
Conditional writes give one-winner semantics without a separate lock service

breaks.d: A long GC pause or slow network lets the lease expire; another node takes the lock while the first still thinks it holds it.
breaks.see: Two writers in the logs for the same lock window
breaks.fix: Fencing tokens checked by the store, plus lease renewal

breaks.d: Redis replication is async, so a promoted replica may not know the lock exists.
breaks.see: Lock granted twice right after a failover
breaks.fix: Consensus store (etcd, ZooKeeper) for correctness locks, or fencing

breaks.d: A plain DEL removes a lock that another client now holds.
breaks.see: Overlapping jobs after a slow run
breaks.fix: Store a random value and delete only if it still matches (DELEX IFEQ or a Lua script)

breaks.d: Redis TTLs use wall-clock time, so a big clock change can end a lock early.
breaks.see: Locks expiring sooner than their TTL
breaks.fix: Run NTP carefully, avoid manual clock changes, rely on fencing

breaks.d: A lock with no TTL, or a session lock left on a pooled connection.
breaks.see: Jobs stuck waiting; one lock held for hours
breaks.fix: Always use a TTL or transaction-scoped locks; alert on long holds

say: Only one scheduler instance should enqueue today's jobs, so each instance tries a lease lock named after the date and the losers simply skip.
The lock is a lease with a TTL that the holder renews, so a crashed holder frees it automatically.
Because a paused process can outlive its lease, every write carries a fencing token and the job table rejects older tokens.
Better still, enqueuing is idempotent with a unique key per job and day, so even a double run creates no duplicates.

followups.a: It is debated. Kleppmann argues it relies on bounded clocks and pauses and offers no fencing tokens, so it should not be used for correctness. Antirez replied with a counterpoint. For correctness, many teams pick etcd or ZooKeeper plus fencing.
A number that rises with each lock grant. The holder sends it with each write and the storage rejects any write with a smaller token than one it has already seen, so a stale holder cannot do damage.
A lock is tied to a lease. The lock key exists while the lease lives; if the lease expires or is revoked, the lock is released and the next waiter is woken.

followups.q: When would you avoid a lock?
followups.a: When the work can be idempotent: a unique constraint, an upsert or a conditional write gives the same safety with no lock service and no lease timing to reason about.

today: Redis 8.4 added DELEX with an IFEQ option, so a lock can be released safely in one command instead of a Lua script.

check.q: A paused process wakes after its lease expired and writes. What stops the damage?
check.a: A fencing token checked by the storage
check.why: The store sees a token older than one it already accepted and rejects the write.

check.q: Why does SET use a random value for a lock?
check.a: So you only delete the lock if it is still yours
d: To make the key expire faster
check.why: Checking the value before deleting stops you removing a lock someone else now holds.

check.q: With Redlock on 5 Redis masters, how many must grant the lock?
check.why: A majority (N/2+1) is needed, so two clients cannot both win.

check.q: Two scheduler copies might both enqueue today's jobs. Simplest safe design?
check.a: Idempotent enqueue with a unique key per job and day
check.why: If a repeat run cannot create duplicates, a lock becomes an optimisation, not a must.
